title: Wei Huang
text: Hi! My name is Wei. I’m from Taiwan and have lived in Vancouver for about 10 years. I’m currently a student in the Master of Data Science and Computational Linguistics program at UBC. Before joining the program, I worked in health research for five years as a researcher and AI developer, implementing LLMs into research workflows. After the program, I hope to apply what I learn to continue on a similar career path, in a more advanced role with more depth and responsibility.

title: GDP and life expectancy in 2007
text:
Data: Gapminder, via the gapminder R package. Licensed CC BY 4.0.
The gapminder dataset contains life expectancy, population, and GDP per capita data for 142 countries from 1952 to 2007. In this post, I explore the correlation between GDP per capita and life expectancy, using data from 2007, the most recent year in the dataset.
library(gapminder)
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)

title: GDP and life expectancy in 2007
text:
Step 1: Filter the data
First, I filter the data to keep only the records from 2007.

gap07 <- gapminder |>
    filter(year == 2007)
gap07

title: GDP and life expectancy in 2007
section: Step 2: Compare median GDP and life expectancy by continent
text:
Step 2: Compare median GDP and life expectancy by continent
Next, I compare the median GDP and life expectancy by continent. Oceania has the highest median GDP and life expectancy, while Africa has the lowest on both.

comparison <- gap07 |>
    group_by(continent) |>
    summarise(
        countries = n(),
        median_gdp = round(median(gdpPercap), 2),
        median_lifeExp = round(median(lifeExp), 2)
    )
comparison

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  continent countries median_gdp median_lifeExp
  <fct>         <int>      <dbl>          <dbl>
1 Africa           52      1452.           52.9
2 Americas         25      8948.           72.9
3 Asia             33      4471.           72.4
4 Europe           30     28054.           78.6
5 Oceania           2     29810.           80.7

title: GDP and life expectancy in 2007
text:
Step 3: Correlation
Then I calculate the correlation between these two variables. The result is 0.68, a fairly strong positive relationship.

corr <- cor(gap07$gdpPercap, gap07$lifeExp)
corr

[1] 0.6786624

title: GDP and life expectancy in 2007
text:
Step 4: Visualization
Finally, I create a scatter plot that shows this positive relationship, with the points coloured by continent to tell them apart. Note that since we have not yet learned about visualization, this snippet is a direct copy from Claude.

   ggplot(gap07, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, colour = continent)) +
    geom_point() +
    labs(x = "GDP per capita (US$)", y = "Life expectancy (years)")







Figure 1: Life expectancy vs. GDP per capita by country, 2007.





The plot shows an interesting pattern. Although the overall relationship is positive, life expectancy rises rapidly among low-income countries, then levels off and remains stable among middle- and high-income countries. Meanwhile, countries with similarly low incomes can have very different life expectancies (e.g., countries in Africa versus Asia). This suggests that other factors besides GDP per capita have a strong influence on life expectancy.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
The first week in MDS was really fun! After working for five years, it was exciting to go back to the classroom and learn. The pace is fast, and the schedule was a bit confusing at first, so I was a little nervous for the first two days.
Thankfully, all the professors and teaching assistants are really nice. They always welcome questions and provide very detailed answers. The classmates are all really kind and supportive too. I’ve made some friends in the first few days, and working with them has been both fun and productive!
Overall, it was a busy but great first week, and I’m excited for what comes next!

title: Do heavier penguins have longer flippers?
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins, collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman at Palmer Station Antarctica LTER, via the palmerpenguins Python package. Licensed CC0.
This dataset contains body measurements for 344 penguins of three species: Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo. The data was collected on three islands in Antarctica from 2007 to 2009. In this post, I explore whether heavier penguins have longer flippers.
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

title: Do heavier penguins have longer flippers?
section: Step 1: Load and clean the data
text:
Step 1: Load and clean the data

penguins = load_penguins()
penguins_clean = penguins.dropna()
print(f"rows before cleaning: {len(penguins)}")
print(f"rows after cleaning: {len(penguins_clean)}")

rows before cleaning: 344
rows after cleaning: 333


Eleven rows have one or more missing values. I excluded them from the analysis, leaving 333 complete rows.

title: Do heavier penguins have longer flippers?
section: Step 2: Compare median body mass and flipper length by species
text:
Step 2: Compare median body mass and flipper length by species
Next, I compare the median body mass and flipper length by species.

comparison = (
    penguins_clean
    .groupby("species")
    .agg(
        penguins=("species", "size"),
        median_body_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "median"),
        median_flipper_length=("flipper_length_mm", "median")
    )
)

The comparison shows that Gentoo penguins are the heaviest and have the longest flippers. Chinstrap and Adelie have the same median weight and similar median flipper length.

title: Do heavier penguins have longer flippers?
text:
Step 3: Analyze the correlation
Then I calculate the correlation between body mass and flipper length.

correlation = round(penguins_clean["body_mass_g"].corr(penguins_clean["flipper_length_mm"]), 2)

correlation

np.float64(0.87)


The correlation is 0.87, a strong positive relationship.

title: Do heavier penguins have longer flippers?
text:
Step 4: Visualization
Finally, I create a scatter plot that shows this correlation, with the points coloured by species to separate them. Note that since we have not yet learned about visualization, this snippet is a direct copy from Claude.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))

for species, group in penguins_clean.groupby("species"):
    ax.scatter(group["flipper_length_mm"], group["body_mass_g"],
                label=species, alpha=0.7)

ax.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.legend(title="Species")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Body mass vs. flipper length of Palmer penguins, by species.





The data shows a strong positive linear relationship between body mass and flipper length: heavier penguins tend to have longer flippers. We can also see that Gentoo penguins are heavier and have longer flippers than the other two species, which are similar to each other in both weight and flipper length.
